Optimizing straw anaerobic digestion via nanobubble technology: Insights 
into hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and methanogenesis processes
Chuanfei Bian a, Hao Liu a, Xin Gao a, Shuaishuai Ma a,c, Xiurong Ren a,  
Muhammad Usman Khan c,d, Luyao Wei a,b, Xufeng Yuan a, Hongliang Wang a,b,  
Wanbin Zhu a,b,*
a Center of Biomass Engineering/College of Agronomy and Biotechnology, China Agricultural University, Beijing, 100193, China
b Sanya Institute of China Agricultural University, Sanya, 572025, China
c Bioproducts, Sciences and Engineering Laboratory, Department of Biological Systems Engineering, Washington State University, 2710 Crimson Way, Richland, WA, 
99354, USA
d Department of Energy Systems Engineering, Faculty of Agricultural Engineering & Technology, University of Agriculture, Faisalabad, Pakistan
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Nanobubble
Straw
Anaerobic digestion
Biomethane production
Microbial community
A B S T R A C T
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is an effective approach for the resource and energy recovery of straw biomass. 
However, the process faces challenges such as poor hydrolysis efficiency, slow startup, and lower overall effi­
ciency. Nanobubble technology offers a promising solution to enhance methane production without causing 
secondary pollution. This study investigates the effects of nanobubble water (NBW) prepared using different 
gases (N2-NBW, O2-NBW, H2-NBW, CO2-NBW, and Air-NBW) on the methane production characteristics and 
microbial communities during AD of corn straw. The results showed that methane production increased by 
11.86 %–24.08 % compared to the control group, with the maximum cumulative methane yield reaching 189.36 
± 5.32 mL/g VS. The modified Gompertz equation effectively fitted the cumulative methane production curves, 
with a high correlation coefficient (R2 > 0.99). Total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS) removal rates improved 
by 9.70 %–26.28 % and 11.87 %–24.09 %, respectively. Microbial community analysis revealed an increased 
relative abundance of bacteria such as Ruminofilibacter, which facilitates hydrolysis and acidogenesis. Addi­
tionally, the relative abundance of methanogenic archaea such as Methanosarcina and Methanobacterium also 
increased to varying degrees. Consequently, the addition of NBW promotes the processes of hydrolysis, aceto­
genesis, and methanogenesis, providing new opportunities for the efficient utilization of straw biomass.
1. Introduction
With growing global energy demand and increasing severity of 
environmental issues, the development of renewable energy has become 
a research hotspot in today’s society [1]. Straw, as a widely distributed 
agricultural waste, has an annual production of approximately 1 billion 
tons in China [2]. Its resource utilization through AD can not only 
reduce environmental pollution but also convert it into cleaner biogas, 
alleviating the dependence on fossil fuels and reducing carbon emissions 
[3,4]. However, the efficient bioconversion of straw is hindered by its 
pronounced recalcitrance, which stems from the complex physico­
chemical structure of lignocellulosic biomass. At the structural level, 
cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin are tightly interwoven to form a 
rigid plant cell wall, creating a natural barrier to microbial and 
enzymatic attack [5]. The high crystallinity of cellulose and the presence 
of extensive hydrogen bonding networks reduce the accessibility of 
hydrolytic enzymes, while hemicellulose acts as a cross-linking matrix 
that further restricts degradation. Lignin, with its highly hydrophobic 
and aromatic polymeric structure, not only provides physical rigidity 
but also exerts non-productive binding with enzymes, thereby inhibiting 
hydrolysis. In addition, the low porosity and limited surface area of 
straw cell walls hinder the penetration of microbial consortia and 
enzymatic systems into the substrate. Collectively, these physicochem­
ical barriers make hydrolysis the rate-limiting step of straw anaerobic 
digestion, emphasizing the need for effective pretreatment and 
enhancement strategies to overcome recalcitrance and improve overall 
bioconversion efficiency [6]. In addition, maintaining a dynamic bal­
ance between hydrolysis and methanogenesis during anaerobic

digestion is a key factor for improving substrate conversion efficiency 
and methane yield [7].
In recent years, many technologies have been developed to increase 
biogas production from straw through AD, aiming to overcome its 
complex and recalcitrant lignocellulosic structure [8]. Nowadays, the 
most common processes for improving lignocellulosic feed-stock 
degradation through AD are chemical (alkaline and acidic), biological 
(fungal or enzyme), oxidative(wet oxidation and wet explosion), and 
physical (milling, extrusion, ultrasonic, steam explosion, and hydro­
thermal treatment) [9]. Even if the lignocellulose’s degradability is 
improved following the aforementioned treatments, each pretreatment 
technique has some pros and cons. For instance, physical pretreatments 
such as milling or steam explosion typically require energy inputs 
ranging from 0.5 to 5 MJ/kg of dry biomass, while chemical pre­
treatments may achieve high cellulose conversion rates (up to 70–80 %) 
but often produce inhibitory compounds such as furfural or generate 
wastewater requiring further treatment [10]. Biological pretreatments 
are generally energy-efficient and environmentally friendly but need 
prolonged processing times (weeks to months) to achieve moderate 
lignin removal (10–30 %). These limitations call for the exploration of 
more effective, energy-efficient, and less chemical-intensive pretreat­
ment methods. Recent advances in biomass utilization technologies 
provide valuable context for such innovations. For example, Sun et al. 
reported a concerted catalysis strategy for bio-ethanol activation and 
dehydrogenation, demonstrating how coordinated chemical and cata­
lytic approaches can significantly enhance biomass conversion effi­
ciency [11]. Building on this perspective of technological innovation, 
nanobubble water (NBW) pretreatment emerges as a promising, 
non-chemical alternative, potentially reducing energy input and chem­
ical usage while maintaining or improving biogas yields. Therefore, 
NBW offers a more sustainable and efficient approach compared with 
existing pretreatment strategies.
NBW is a special liquid form containing a large number of 
nanometer-sized bubbles (with diameters less than 1 μm), generated in 
water through methods such as mechanical agitation [12], hydrody­
namic cavitation [13], ultrasonic cavitation [14], and membrane 
filtration [15]. Because of this, it possesses more reactive oxygen species 
(ROS), a greater specific surface area, a faster mass transfer efficiency, a 
longer residence time, a higher surface charge, and stronger gas solu­
bility, among other characteristics [16,17]. However, NBWs also exhibit 
potential instability over time, and their large-scale generation may 
involve operational complexity and significant energy requirements, 
which need to be critically considered for practical applications [18]. In 
recent years, NBW has been widely applied in fields such as wastewater 
treatment, soil improvement, aquaculture, and waste treatment [18]. 
Recent studies have shown that NBW also has a significant positive ef­
fect on the AD process. It can increase methane production and promote 
substrate degradation, while also not causing secondary pollution after 
use, offering excellent environmental benefits [19]. The mechanisms by 
which NBW formed from different gases (such as nitrogen, oxygen, 
hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and air) affect microorganisms during AD in a 
different way. For example, N2-NBW provides an inert gas environment, 
reducing the inhibitory effects of dissolved oxygen on anaerobic bacteria 
[20]. O2-NBW can improve the hydrolysis and acidogenesis processes in 
the early stages. The collapse of the bubbles may generate small amounts 
of reactive oxygen species (such as hydroxyl radicals), which help pro­
mote the opening or oxidation of refractory substances [21]. H2-NBW 
can provide a hydrogen source, promoting the activity of 
hydrogen-producing bacteria and methane-producing bacteria [22]; 
CO2- may participate in the carbon cycle, enhancing the activity of 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens and increasing the methane production 
rate [23]; Air-NBW’s nitrogen and oxygen increase the gas exchange 
efficiency in the liquid phase, enhancing mass transfer efficiency [24]. 
However, these reported effects may be influenced by potential insta­
bility of NBWs, operational challenges, and the energy requirements for 
large-scale generation, which should be critically considered. Thus, it is 
crucial from both a theoretical and practical standpoint to investigate 
how different kinds of NBW affect different stages of straw AD.
Despite these promising findings, current research on the application 
of different NBW types in AD is still in its infancy. Most existing studies 
focus on single-gas NBW treatments, lacking a systematic comparison of 
the effects of various gas-based NBWs under identical conditions. 
Moreover, comprehensive evaluations of how these treatments influence 
the microbial community structure and functional metabolism during 
different AD stages are still scarce. In addition, previous work has rarely 
extended beyond overall performance measurements, with limited 
exploration of how NBWs regulate microbial community dynamics and 
functional metabolism across the distinct stages of hydrolysis, acido­
genesis, and methanogenesis. This lack of comparative and mechanistic 
insights constitutes a critical knowledge gap that hampers the rational 
design and optimization of NBW-assisted AD systems.
To fill this knowledge gap, this study systematically investigates the 
impact of NBWs formed from different gases (N2, O2, H2, CO2, and air) 
on the anaerobic digestion of straw. Specifically, the study aims to (i) 
evaluate their effects on hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and methanogenesis; 
(ii) analyze changes in microbial community composition using high- 
throughput sequencing; and (iii) elucidate the functional mechanisms 
via predictive metabolic analysis. We hypothesize that different gas- 
based NBWs will exert distinct effects on the key stages of anaerobic 
digestion, that they will modulate microbial community composition 
and functional metabolism in a gas-dependent manner, and that these 
microbial and metabolic shifts will underpin the enhanced methane 
production observed in NBW-assisted systems. The ultimate goal is to 
provide an efficient, non-toxic, and environmentally friendly strategy 
for enhancing biogas production from lignocellulosic biomass.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
Corn straw collected from the Shangzhuang Experimental Station, 
Haidian District, Beijing, China, and used as a feedstock in this study. 
The substrate was initially sun-dried after collection, coarsely ground to 
a particle size of 2 mm, and then washed thoroughly to remove dust and 
other impurities. Subsequently, it was further dried in an oven main­
tained at 60 ◦C and finally milled to a 60-mesh particle size for subse­
quent use. The inoculum used in this study was collected from a 
continuous mesophilic (37 ◦C) AD reactor using cow dung and straw as 
feedstock. The inoculum was stored in a 4 ◦C refrigerator after collection 
for subsequent use. To eliminate the influence of residual degradable 
materials in the inoculum, it was placed in a 37 ◦C incubator and fer­
mented until no more gas production was observed before the experi­
ment. The physicochemical properties of the corn straw and inoculum 
are shown in Table 1.

2.2. Preparation of NBW
NBW was generated in a nanobubble generator (ZJC-NM, Shanghai 
Zhongjing Environmental Protection Technology Co., Ltd.), which 
operates on the principle of pressurized gas dissolution, as described in 
previous studies [25]. The operating conditions of the generator were as 
follows: gas flow rate of 0.12 L/min, deionized water (DW) flow rate of 
3 L/min, operating pressure of 0.38–0.40 MPa, and a running time of 10 
min [25].
2.3. Batch biochemical methane potential (BMP) test
The batch AD experiments were carried out in serum bottles with a 
total volume of 250 mL, with an effective volume of 200 mL. The VS 
content was set to 5 %, and the substrate-to-inoculum ratio was 2:1. 
Deionized water was used as the control group(CK), and N2-NBW, O2- 
NBW, H2-NBW, CO2-NBW, and Air-NBW were used as experimental 
groups, added to the anaerobic fermentation experiments. To eliminate 
the biogas produced by the inoculated sludge itself, a blank control 
containing an equal amount of sludge was included. After loading all 
materials, the pH was adjusted to around 7 using HCl and NaOH, and the 
bottles were sealed with rubber stoppers and aluminum caps. All re­
actors were flushed with N2 for 3 min, and then, based on preliminary 
experiments, the reactors were incubated at 35 ± 1 ◦C for 28 days. Each 
test was performed in triplicates and the average results were used. 
Before measuring the gas production, the bottles were manually shaken 
for 3 min at a fixed time each day.
2.4. Analysis methods
The pH value, TS, VS, and soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) 
were analyzed following established standard methods(APHA, 2012) 
[26]. The contents of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin were quanti­
fied according to procedures described in previous studies [27]. The 
biogas composition was analyzed using a GC-2014 (Shimadzu, Japan) 
with a 2 m × 4 mm BP1 chromatographic column, operating at a pres­
sure of 1.3 MPa. A hydrogen flame ionization detector was used with a 
flow rate of 25 mL/min. The detector temperatures were set at 40 ◦C and 
100 ◦C. The detection time was 1.5 min with a 300 μL air sample. For the 
qualitative and quantitative analysis of VFAs (lactic acid, formic acid, 
acetic acid, and propionic acid) in the samples, high-performance liquid 
chromatography (LC-20A, Shimadzu, Japan) with the external standard 
method was employed. The chromatographic column used was Aminex 
HPX-87H(300 mm × 7.8 mm), with a mobile phase of 5 mM H2SO4 and a 
flow rate of 0.6 mL/min. The column oven was set at 40 ◦C, with an 
injection volume of 10 μL. The detector was SPD-S20A, with an absor­
bance wavelength of 205 nm, and the detection time was 30 min.
2.5. AD kinetic models
The cumulative methane production data were fitted using a modi­
fied Gompertz model to obtain parameters such as the lag phase, 
maximum methane production rate, and the fitted maximum methane 
yield (Equation (1)). The Logistic model is commonly used to describe 
the dynamic behavior of methane production, reflecting the rapid 
growth in the early phase, a slowdown in the middle phase, and stabi­
lization in the later phase of gas production (Equation (2)). The first- 
order hydrolysis kinetic model simulates the hydrolysis process during 
fermentation based on the balance between organic matter degradation 
and methane production (Equation (3)).

2.6. Microbial community analysis
The samples were dispatched to Shanghai Meiji Biotechnology Co., 
Ltd. for analysis, where high-throughput sequencing of the 16S rRNA 
gene was subsequently conducted on the Illumina MiSeq platform. The 
bacterial amplification primers were 338F and 806R, and the archaeal 
amplification primers were 524F10extF and Arch958RmodR. A series of 
microbial-related analyses were conducted using the Meiji Cloud plat­
form, and PICRUSt2 was employed to predict microbial metabolic 
functions and identify key enzymes [28]. Functional annotation of the 
results was carried out using the KEGG database (https://www.genome. 
jp/kegg/). Finally, the raw data generated from the microbial 
sequencing was uploaded to the NCBI database (https://www.ncbi.nlm. 
nih.gov), with the accession number PRJNA1169782.
2.7. Statistical analysis
Data statistics were performed using Excel 2010 (Microsoft Corp., 
Redmond, USA), and data processing and analysis were conducted using 
SPSS 25.0 (IBM, USA), with statistical significance set at p < 0.05p <
0.05. Model plotting was done using Origin 2021 (OriginLab Corp., 
Northampton, USA).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effect of NBW on methane production
Methane production is commonly considered an important indicator 
for evaluating the effectiveness of AD [27]. As shown in Fig. 1a, the gas 
production process from corn straw exhibits three peak periods, corre­
sponding to the effective utilization of soluble organic matter (2 days), 
cellulose (8 days), and hemicellulose and other substances (18 days). 
Fig. 1b displays the methane contents of all samples, with overall dif­
ferences in methane content among the different NBW treatment groups 
being relatively small. Fig. 1c shows the cumulative methane production 
curve, clearly indicating that the addition of NBW significantly 
increased methane production (p < 0.05). Specifically, the cumulative 
methane production in the N2-NBW, O2-NBW, H2-NBW, CO2-NBW, and 
Air-NBW treatment groups was 176.94 ± 3.27, 170.72 ± 5.14, 186.17 
± 3.31, 189.36 ± 5.32, and 179.95 ± 5.22 mL/g VS, respectively, which 
is an increase of 15.94 %, 11.86 %, 21.99 %, 24.08 %, and 17.92 % 
compared to the CK (DW, 152.61 ± 1.77 mL/g VS) (Fig. 1d). Among 
these, CO2-NBW showed the highest methane production, with its lower 
pH creating acidic conditions during straw anaerobic digestion, pro­
moting the hydrolysis and acidogenesis processes, and providing sub­
strates for the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway, ultimately 
achieving the highest methane production. This finding is consistent 
with previous studies that demonstrated the effectiveness of

CO2-enriched nanobubble water in enhancing methanogenesis by 
stimulating hydrolysis and shifting the methanogenic pathway toward 
hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis [19,25]. Similarly, H2-NBW, by 
providing H2 as a substrate for hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis, also 
resulted in higher methane production. This finding is consistent with 
those of other researchers [22]. A significant methane yield improve­
ment was also observed in the AD system using Air-NBW. Although the 
presence of air usually leads to the death of methane-producing bacteria, 
under actual AD conditions, the limited oxygen is quickly consumed by 
aerobic microorganisms or facultative anaerobes, rapidly transitioning 
the reaction environment to anaerobic [29]. In addition, some 
methane-producing bacteria have a certain tolerance to oxygen, and 
after the inhibition from oxygen exposure is removed, their biological 
activity can quickly recover. Therefore, Air-NBW has a significantly 
greater promoting effect on AD compared to CK with distilled water. The 
presence of limited oxygen can stimulate the proliferation of 
lignocellulose-degrading microorganisms, thereby accelerating the 
breakdown of lignocellulose—a key factor in enhancing the hydrolysis 
efficiency of anaerobic digestion. Furthermore, N2-NBW helps maintain 
a strict anaerobic environment, preventing the inactivation of anaerobic 
bacteria due to fluctuations in dissolved oxygen and improving methane 
production by enhancing mass transfer efficiency. With long-term use, 
N2-NBW can provide more stable conditions for AD, further contributing 
to improved methane production.
To more comprehensively analyze the kinetic characteristics of the 
anaerobic fermentation process with different types of NBW or distilled 
water (DW), this study applied the modified Gompertz model, Logistic 
model, and first-order hydrolysis kinetic model to fit the data, with 
relevant parameters shown in Table 2. The modified Gompertz and 
Logistic models are widely applied to describe cumulative methane 
production because they can capture the sigmoidal pattern of biogas 
generation and provide reliable estimates of the methane production 
potential, maximum production rate, and lag phase. In contrast, the 
first-order hydrolysis kinetic model assumes that substrate hydrolysis is 
the rate-limiting step of anaerobic digestion and thus focuses on the 
degradation kinetics of organic matter. The combined use of these 
models allows both empirical fitting of methane production behavior 
and mechanistic interpretation of substrate degradation. The results

showed that the modified Gompertz model had a better fit (R2 =
0.9901–0.9966) compared to the Logistic model (R2 = 0.9647–0.9937) 
and the first-order hydrolysis kinetic model (R2 = 0.8408–0.9461). This 
model was used to fit the cumulative methane production, and the ob­
tained parameters included the final methane production (Pmax), 
maximum methane production rate (Rmax), and lag phase (λ). The re­
sults indicated that the predicted final methane production was in close 
agreement with the actual measured values. The predicted final 
methane production closely matched the actual measured values, con­
firming the model’s reliability.The lag phase parameter (λ) represents 
the initial period before microorganisms adapt to the new environment, 
proliferate, and enter the exponential growth phase. Generally, a larger 
λ indicates slower microbial adaptation, delayed enzymatic activity, or 
the time required to remove inhibitory compounds, resulting in a slower 
onset of methane production [30]. Comparing λ values among treat­
ments, DW exhibited a lag phase of 3.29 days, while O2-NBW (3.12 days) 
and Air-NBW (2.92 days) showed shorter lag phases, suggesting that 
these treatments accelerated microbial adaptation and enzyme activa­
tion. The presence of oxygen in O2-NBW and Air-NBW likely promotes 
electron transfer, stimulates reactive oxygen species generation, and 
enhances the activity of hydrolytic and acidogenic enzymes, facilitating 
faster substrate breakdown [29]. In contrast, H2-NBW (3.37 days) and 
CO2-NBW (3.85 days) displayed longer lag phases, indicating slower 
initial fermentation. This may result from transient inhibitory effects of 
dissolved hydrogen or carbon dioxide on specific microbial populations, 
which delay the establishment of active methanogenic consortia, 
although these gases could enhance methane production in later stages. 
Overall, these findings suggest that NBW not only accelerates methane 
production but also modulates microbial community dynamics and 
functional metabolism during the lag phase. The type of gas and its in­
teractions with microbial adaptation and environmental conditions play 
key roles in determining the duration of the lag phase and the subse­
quent efficiency of anaerobic digestion.
3.2. Changes in VFAs, pH, SCOD, and TS/VS removal rates during AD
In the AD system, pH is a comprehensive reflection of various 
biochemical reactions, including CO2 dissolution equilibrium, acid-base 
balance, and ion dissolution equilibrium [31]. According to the litera­
ture, the pH range suitable for the growth and metabolism of 
methane-producing bacteria is 6.5–8.2. The pH values of all experi­
mental groups in the first two days ranged from 6.68 to 7.02, which were 
lower than the subsequent pH levels. This indicates that during this 
period, due to the microbial hydrolysis and acidogenesis processes, 
soluble substances and lignocellulose were decomposed, producing 
lactic acid, which was gradually converted into short-chain fatty acids, 
primarily including formic acid, acetic acid, and propionic acid (Fig. 2a). 
During a typical methane production process, short-chain volatile fatty 
acids are progressively consumed by methanogenic archaea, resulting in 
a gradual decline in their concentrations. In the experiment, the TVFA 
concentrations in the CK and treatment groups ranged from 295.33 to 
5741.34 mg/L and 378.12–8592.67 mg/L, respectively. The incorpo­
ration of NBW facilitates the degradation of organic compounds in the 
straw and promotes the formation of soluble substances, thereby 
significantly enhancing acid production efficiency [32]. Notably, the 
TVFA concentration in the CO2-NBW treatment group (452.10–8784.13 
mg/L) was significantly higher than that in the other experimental 
groups, and its pH was lower than that of the others due to high con­
centrations of VFAs. This enhanced the metabolic activity in the 
acidogenesis phase, accelerated the acidification reaction, and conse­
quently lowered the pH of the system [23]. This mechanism suggests 
that CO2-NBW can effectively enhance hydrolysis and acid production 
efficiency by regulating the acidification environment, providing a new 
approach for optimizing the AD process [25].
SCOD is typically used to evaluate substrate solubility during the 
hydrolysis process [33]. The trend in SCOD changes was similar to that 
of TVFA concentrations (Fig. 2b), with all treatment groups showing an 
initial increase followed by a decrease. On day 5, SCOD reached its 
maximum value, which may have been due to the release of a large 
amount of volatile fatty acids (VFA) during the hydrolysis phase. 
However, at this point, the SCOD in the NBW treatment groups was 
lower than that in the DW control group, indicating that after adding 
NBW, soluble organic matter was consumed more rapidly by microor­
ganisms in the AD process, being used for metabolism and gas produc­
tion. Starting from day 5, the SCOD in all treatment groups gradually 
decreased, further indicating that the soluble organic matter had been 
effectively utilized by the digestion system, converting it into methane 
and other metabolic products [34].

degree of substrate degradation. Typically, the degradation rates of TS

and VS are positively correlated with methane production [35]. As 
shown in Fig. 2b, the TS and VS removal rates in the treatment groups 
ranged from 50.22 % to 57.81 % and 42.68 %–47.34 %, respectively, 
which were significantly higher than those in the CK (TS: 45.78 %, VS: 
38.15 %) (p < 0.05). Among these, the CO2-NBW treatment group 
exhibited the highest TS and VS removal rates, at 57.81 % and 47.34 %, 
respectively, which were 26.28 % and 24.09 % higher than those in the 
CK. This result is consistent with the highest cumulative methane pro­
duction observed in this group (Fig. 2b) and is also in agreement with 
previous studies reporting that CO2 nanobubble water can enhance 
organic matter degradation and methane yield during anaerobic diges­
tion [23]. In summary, adding NBW can increase the substrate’s hy­
drolysis and acidogenesis efficiency, which will raise the rate of VS 
degradation and, eventually, methane production [36].
3.3. Effects of NBW on microbial community structure and metabolic 
functions
High-throughput sequencing analysis was conducted to further 
explore the mechanisms of NBW and to elucidate the microbial com­
munity structure changes under different NBW treatments. The results of 
the Alpha diversity analysis for bacteria and archaea are shown in 
Table 3, with coverage indices exceeding 0.99, indicating that the 
sequencing data adequately represent the true diversity of the microbial 
communities in the samples. The diversity of the biological communities 
was evaluated using the Shannon and Simpson indices [37], whilst the 
microbial community richness was reflected using the Ace and Chao 
indices [38].
In the bacterial sequencing, the Sobs index, Chao index, and Ace 
index indicated that the microbial community abundance in O2-NBW 
and Air-NBW was higher than the CK and N2-NBW. This may be because 
oxygen promotes the growth of certain facultative anaerobic microor­
ganisms, suggesting that trace amounts of oxygen are beneficial for 
improving the performance of bacterial microbial communities in the 
AD process. Compared to the bacterial community, the richness index of 
archaea was significantly lower [39]. The Sobs value in the CK was the 
lowest (20), while the Sobs values for CO2-NBW and H2-NBW were the 
highest (28 and 26, respectively). In environments with carbon dioxide 
and hydrogen (CO2-NBW, H2-NBW), the richness of archaea was slightly 
higher.
The results of the Shannon and Simpson indices indicate that, in the 
bacterial community, aerobic environments (such as Air-NBW and O2- 
NBW) promoted the diversity of the community while increasing 
evenness. This suggests that different types of bacteria are able to coexist 
and grow together in these environments [40]. In the archaeal com­
munity, the carbon dioxide environment was beneficial for increasing 
both diversity and evenness, while the hydrogen environment led to 
certain archaeal species dominating. This may be due to the strong 
adaptability and competitiveness of specific archaea to hydrogen.
3.3.1. Dominant bacterial community
The dominant phyla are Bacteroidota and Firmicutes, which are also 
the two most common phyla in AD (Fig. 3a) [41]. Bacteroidota domi­
nates the hydrolysis and primary fermentation stages, responsible for 
converting complex organic matter (such as polysaccharides and pro­
teins) into simple small molecules and volatile fatty acids [42]. The 
highest abundance of Bacteroidota was observed in CO2-NBW, suggest­
ing that CO2 may influence the pH environment of the system, thereby 
regulating the microbial community structure. Firmicutes include many 
strict anaerobes and hydrogen-producing bacteria, which can utilize 
hydrogen as an electron donor to participate in metabolism [43]. These 
bacteria produce cellulases, proteases, and various extracellular en­
zymes to degrade complex organic matter [44]. H2-NBW, by releasing a 
high concentration of dissolved hydrogen, provides abundant hydrogen 
resources, significantly promoting the growth and metabolic activity of 
these bacterial species. As a result, this phylum had the highest abun­
dance in H2-NBW. At the genus level (Fig. 3b), Ruminofilibacter had the 
highest abundance, and it is typically found in the rumen of ruminant 
animals. Ruminofilibacter is capable of degrading cellulose and con­
verting it into short-chain fatty acids [45]. In CO2-NBW, Ruminofilibacter 
had the highest proportion, possibly directly participating in the cellu­
lose degradation metabolic pathway, promoting substrate conversion 
and microbial growth. It may also collaborate with hydrogen-producing 
bacteria to provide sufficient substrates for methane-producing bacteria 
(CO2 + H2 → CH4), forming a mutualistic relationship. This metabolic 
network may further enhance the activity of Ruminofilibacter.
3.3.2. Dominant Archaeal Community
Compared to the bacterial community, the archaeal community 
exhibited significantly lower diversity and richness. During the meth­
anogenesis stage, different archaea play key roles in methane produc­
tion. At the phylum level, Halobacterota and Euryarchaeota dominated, 
with their combined relative abundance accounting for 96.95 %–99.95 
% of the total relative abundance at the phylum level (Fig. 3c). At the 
genus level, Methanosarcina and Methanobacterium were the dominant 
genera (Fig. 3d). Methanosarcina is a commonly observed acetoclastic 
methanogen in methane production systems and was enriched across all 
groups. In addition, Methanobacterium is a hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogen whose primary energy sources are CO2 and H2 [46]. Its enrich­
ment was higher in the CO2-NBW group compared to the CK, indicating 
that CO2-NBW primarily relies on the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis 
pathway.
To further evaluate the metabolic responses mediated by different 
NBWs during AD of straw, the relative abundances of key enzyme genes 
using KEGG metabolic pathways (Fig. 4). In the hydrolysis-acidogenesis 
stage (Fig. 4a), the enzyme levels across the groups were observed 
(Fig. 4b). Compared to the CK, CO2-NBW showed a decrease in cellulase 
(EC: 3.2.1.4) involved in the hydrolysis of cellulose to glucose, while 
β-glucosidase (EC:3.2.1.21) increased. Similarly, xylanase (EC: 3.2.1.8) 
was involved in the hydrolysis of hemicellulose to xylulose decreased,

3.4. Preliminary analysis of the promoting mechanisms of different NBWs
Different types of NBW, through their unique gas dissolution char­
acteristics and gas-liquid interface behavior, promote the hydrolysis, 
acidogenesis, and methanogenesis stages. Among them, CO2-NBW ex­
erts the most significant promoting effect by regulating the acidification 
environment, providing carbon sources, and promoting the enrichment 
of hydrogenotrophic methanogens like Methanobacterium. H2-NBW, by 
providing substrates for the hydrogenotrophic pathway, also has a 
strong advantage in the methanogenesis phase. In contrast, N2-NBW, O2- 
NBW, and Air-NBW primarily affect the hydrolysis and acidogenesis 
stages in the early fermentation phase. These observations suggest that 
the role of NBW is not limited to simply enhancing gas–liquid mass 
transfer, but also involves modifying the microbial community structure 
and the metabolic balance among different functional groups. For 
instance, the stimulation of hydrogenotrophic methanogens under CO2- 
NBW and H2-NBW treatments indicates that nanobubbles may act as 
selective regulators, favoring specific methanogenic pathways. Simi­
larly, the improved hydrolysis and acidogenesis under O2-NBW and Air- 
NBW imply that small amounts of oxygen could enhance extracellular 
enzyme activity and accelerate the breakdown of complex substrates. 
Although preliminary, these findings provide mechanistic clues as to 
why different gases lead to divergent promoting effects. They also 
highlight that the choice of NBW type could be tailored to target specific 
stages of anaerobic digestion, thereby offering a flexible strategy for 
process optimization. These mechanisms provide diversified regulatory 
strategies for optimizing straw anaerobic fermentation and offer theo­
retical support for NBW selection and process improvements in practical 
applications. Future studies should examine how substrate heterogene­
ity, operational parameters (e.g., organic loading rate, temperature, 
pH), and potential non-biological effects (e.g., mass transfer, micro- 
mixing, mechanical disruption) influence AD, as well as their impacts 
on effluent quality, nutrient balance, and downstream process stability, 
to fully assess the practical applicability of NBW.
4. Conclusion
In this study, NBWs prepared with different gas types all enhanced 
the hydrolysis-acidogenesis degree and degradation rate of straw, and 
optimized the functional microbial community structure in hydrolysis, 
acidogenesis, and methanogenesis, thereby improving the methane 
production efficiency from straw. Among them, the cumulative methane 
production in the N2-NBW, O2-NBW, H2-NBW, CO2-NBW, and Air-NBW 
treatment groups increased by 11.86 %–24.08 % compared to the CK. 
The TS and VS removal rates increased by 9.70 %–26.28 % and 11.87 %– 
24.09 %, respectively. CO2-NBW showed the best results with maximum 
methane reaching 189.36 ± 5.32 mL/g VS, specifically enhancing the 
expression of enzymes involved in hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis. 
In conclusion, utilizing nanobubble technology to stabilize different 
gases for generating NBWs can enhance methane production in corn 
straw AD. The purpose of this study is to offer some references for the use 
of nanobubble technology in AD to promote the synthesis of methane 
from straw biomass.
